sentences: So you can tell what each new thing does, add them one at a time, starting with the UMP trial and working down the list below to the keto diet.
5-HTP could help your mood here, though iboga acts on serotonin too, so don't take 5-HTP at all while you're microdosing iboga or elliptica.

But if you want UMP with any microdose, or 5-HTP with a mushroom microdose, there isn't enough data yet to say whether the warnings against taking these supplements on psychedelic days apply to microdose days.
So until there's more data, you can try the one you want each way, on a microdose day and a day without, to see how it feels.
If you're too numb to tell, compare your sleep and dreams on the nights after each kind of day.
Like iboga, mushrooms act on serotonin, so stop the 5-HTP if you get any of the stop signs the 5-HTP section lists.

fable: Every sentence is built the same way, a condition or reason followed by "so" plus an instruction ("So you can tell", "so don't take", "So until", "so stop"), and nearly every one opens with a connective (So, But, So, If, Like). The reasoning is airtight and evenly paced, with each sentence about the same length and no aside or loose end, which makes it read as assembled more than spoken.
haiku: The paragraph runs on evenly balanced clauses, with each caveat followed by a tidy resolution and a parallel pair ("UMP with any microdose, or 5-HTP with a mushroom microdose"), which gives it a rhythm of hedge, then fix, then hedge again. Its voice is neutral and instructional, and it is built as a checklist of conditionals rather than a personal account.
sonnet: Every sentence is a similar medium length with a clean logical connective ("So", "But", "though", "So until", "so"), and the paragraph walks through each case in order, so it has the even, exhaustively covered rhythm of an assistant writing safety guidance. The voice is steady and impersonal, with no digressions, asides or uneven emphasis.
